Here is what comes.

The cursor blinks on the blank page like a metronome, steady and patient, asking me to fill the silence. I don't know what I want to say. I think that’s all right. Sometimes the best things start as a fog, a low gray mass that doesn’t look like anything from the outside, but inside there is moisture, movement, the possibility of rain. I sit here with a thousand words to spend, which feels like both a fortune and a burden. How do you spend a fortune wisely? Maybe you don’t. Maybe you just spend it, letting it scatter like coins into a fountain, each one a small wish.

I think of rain, of how it sounds on a tin roof, how it turns dust into mud and mud into memory. When I was a child, I believed the rain was the sky crying, and I would ask my mother what it was sad about. She would smile and say, “Maybe it’s not sad. Maybe it’s just full.” I never forgot that. Fullness can spill over, can become something that looks like grief but is really just an overflow of living. I want to be like that—not leaking from sadness, but brimming with too much world, too much wonder, until the excess runs down my face in silver lines.

There is a certain freedom in writing without a map. No thesis, no plot, no promised destination. Just words stacking on words like stones in a dry creek bed, making a path that may lead nowhere or everywhere. I think about how many thoughts pass through a mind in a single day, how most of them evaporate like morning dew. To catch even a fraction of them in language is a miracle. It is like trying to hold a river in a jar. You don’t get the whole river, but you get the coldness of it, the movement, a small body of truth that you can carry with you.

Yesterday I saw a squirrel on the wire fence, balancing with its tail like a dancer. It stopped, looked at me, and for a moment we shared a strange acknowledgment: two animals aware of each other, both uncertain, both curious. Then it dashed away, and I felt oddly lonely. So much of life is like that—brief connections that come and go, leaving only a faint warmth. I wonder if the squirrel remembers me. I wonder if it has a word for “human” in its chittering language, or if I am just a shape, a shadow, a thing that passed through its territory. We are all just shapes to each other, until we learn each other’s names.

Language is a net. It lets us catch some things, but it also leaves gaps. The thing about love—how do you net that? The smell of rain on pavement? The ache of missing someone before they’ve even left? Some experiences slip through the mesh, too fine for words. And yet we keep trying. We build poems and songs, we send text messages with emojis and ellipses, we whisper in the dark hoping the other person understands. Perhaps that is the most human thing we do: we strain the ocean of existence through a net of letters, and we share what little we catch.

My grandmother’s kitchen had a particular smell: yeast, cinnamon, wood smoke, and something sweetly floral from the soap she kept by the sink. I can summon it now, many years later, just by closing my eyes. Memory is not in the brain alone. It is in the nose, the tongue, the skin. When I think of her, I think of her hands, dough-covered and scarred, pressing shapes into cookies. She never wrote anything down. Her recipes lived in her fingers, in the rhythm of her rolling pin, in the patience of her waiting for the dough to rise. I wonder if I have inherited some of that rhythm, that patience, that ability to make something from flour and water and time.

In the distance, a train whistle cuts through the afternoon. It is a lonely sound, the kind that makes you look out the window even though you know you can’t see the tracks from here. I have never ridden a train across the country, but I imagine it: the landscape unrolling like a scroll, the names of towns flashing past—places I will never visit, lives I will never live. That is what the whistle promises: another world, just over the horizon. And even if I never go, the promise itself is enough. It reminds me that there is always more, that the map of my own life is only a small square in a vast atlas.

We are made of stories, the ones we tell and the ones we keep hidden. I have a secret drawer in my heart filled with memories I don’t know how to share. Some are too bright, too sharp; they would cut the listener. Others are too tender, like a bruise that hasn’t healed. But I think the secret drawer is necessary. Not everything needs to be spoken. Some stories are meant only for the self, to be revisited in quiet moments, to be folded and unfolded until they become soft. Still, I write them down sometimes, buried in a notebook no one will ever read. It is a way of honoring them, of giving them a body made of ink.

Somewhere a clock ticks, but I don’t know whose. Time is so strange. It moves at the same speed for everyone, yet it feels different. A minute with a burning hand is forever. An hour with a friend is a breath. I try not to waste time, but what is waste? Writing this—was it a waste? If no one reads it, does it still exist? I think yes. The act of thinking, of shaping thought into sentences, is a kind of living. It is a way of paying attention, of saying to the universe: I was here, I noticed this, I turned it into something. Maybe that is enough. Maybe that is all any of us can do.

The page is not empty anymore. It is filled with my rambling, my small observations, my half-formed thoughts. A thousand words is both a long way and a short one. I have come to the end, but also to a beginning. Because this is not really a conclusion; it is just a pause. The cursor still blinks, ready for more. And I will give it more, if not now, then later. There is always more. There is always another thought, another rain, another squirrel on the fence, another train whistle calling from the distance. I am just a person with a keyboard, trying to hold the river, knowing I will fail, but grateful for the coldness in my hands. That is what comes. And it is enough.
